periods.label: Late Medieval
periods.narrative: The later Middle Ages open under the shadow of the Black Death (from 1347) and close toward gunpowder states and Renaissance courts. England and France bleed through the Hundred Years’ War; the Avignon papacy and Schism fracture Latin Christendom’s prestige; Burgundy flowers as a princely superpower; Iberian crowns push Granada; the Ottomans cross into Europe and crush Serbian and Byzantine power toward 1453; Poland and Lithuania join in personal union against the Teutonic Order and the steppe; Muscovy gathers Russian lands after the Golden Horde’s weakening. Culture: Gothic perpendicular and Flamboyant, vernacular literature (Chaucer, Dante’s afterlife, chivalric orders), and intensified devotional religion. Genetics: plague kills on a vast scale but does not invent new deep components — regional continua persist with mobility along war and trade.
periods.culturesNote: Hundred Years’ War realms; Burgundy; Crown of Aragon & Castile; Holy Roman mosaic; Jagiellon Poland–Lithuania; Ottoman Rumelia; Muscovy; Italian city-states.

iberia.description: Castile and Aragon (with Catalonia and Valencia) dominate Christian Iberia; Portugal is an Atlantic kingdom; Nasrid Granada survives as Islam’s last Iberian foothold under tribute and raid. Courtly culture mixes crusading ideology with Mediterranean commerce. Jewish and Muslim minorities remain crucial — and increasingly precarious — to urban economies. Ancestry is medieval Iberian continua with North African and earlier layers; politics is dynastic union building toward the Catholic Monarchs.
iberia.languages: Castilian, Portuguese, Catalan, etc.; Andalusi Arabic; Basque; Latin/Hebrew in domains
iberia.linguisticNote: Romance victory narrative with lasting Arabic loanwords and toponyms.
iberia.ancestryNote: Shifting clines from medieval contact; post-conquest homogenization incomplete.

britain.description: Plantagenet and then Lancastrian England fights for the French crown while Welsh revolt (Owain Glyndŵr) and Scottish wars flare. The Black Death empties manors and raises labor’s price; vernacular English (Chaucer) claims literary prestige beside French and Latin. Ireland remains a patchwork of English pale and Gaelic lordships. Genetics: plague mortality and mobility, not a new ancestral strand — continuity from high medieval Britain with aristocratic French ties.
britain.languages: Middle English; Anglo-Norman French; Welsh/Gaelic/Scots/etc.; Latin
britain.linguisticNote: Trilingual elite culture; English re-emerges as state language later.
britain.ancestryNote: Elite Norman layer; majority continuity from early medieval England.

france.description: Valois France fractures under English occupation, civil war (Armagnac–Burgundian), and Jacquerie social revolt, then slowly reconsolidates with gunpowder, taxes, and Joan of Arc’s mythic campaign. Burgundy’s dukes build a glittering state from Flanders to the Jura. Cathedrals, mystery plays, and royal sacral ideology define culture. Demography rebounds unevenly after plague on a Frankish–medieval French gene pool.
france.languages: Old/Middle French; Occitan; Breton; Basque edge; Latin
france.linguisticNote: Langue d’oïl vs oc is a major internal linguistic divide.
france.ancestryNote: Medieval France continuity; north/south structure persists.

central.description: The Holy Roman Empire is elective and plural: Luxemburg and early Habsburg emperors, Bohemian crown lands heading toward Hussite revolution, Swiss confederate victories, Teutonic Order vs Poland–Lithuania (Grünwald/Tannenberg 1410). German towns of the Hansa knit the Baltic. Latin and German law, Gothic art, and university theology (Prague, Vienna) shape elite culture. Ancestry: central European medieval continua.
central.languages: Middle High German; Czech/Polish/etc.; Italian vernaculars; Latin; Hungarian in the basin
central.linguisticNote: Empire ≠ one language; Latin and German as linking codes.
central.ancestryNote: German–Slavic contact zones show admixture; alpine/italian lands differ.

scandinavia.description: The Kalmar Union (from 1397) binds Denmark, Norway, and Sweden under one monarch in theory, with Swedish resistance never far away. Hanseatic merchants dominate Bergen and Baltic trade; Norwegian royal power wanes. Christianity is firmly Latin; vernacular laws and sagas persist in manuscript. Genetics track Nordic medieval populations — union is political, not a population replacement.
scandinavia.linguisticNote: From Old Norse relative unity to separate medieval standards.
scandinavia.ancestryNote: Continuous with Viking Age Nordic ternary; Christian medieval kingdoms are political-cultural, not a new genetic pulse.

italy.description: Visconti Milan, republican Florence, papal states, Naples, and maritime Venice/Genoa invent Renaissance patronage even before 1400’s end — humanism, vernacular epic, and mercenary condottieri. The south remains an Angevin then Aragonese prize. Urban density and plague shape demography; ancestry is Italian medieval continua with eastern Mediterranean trade contacts.
italy.languages: Italian dialects/volgare; Latin; Greek remnants in south
italy.linguisticNote: Dante’s era crystallizes literary Italian on a dialect continuum.
italy.ancestryNote: Ports cosmopolitan; hinterlands more local medieval Italian.

balkans.description: Serbian power peaks then falters (Kosovo 1389 in memory and politics); Bulgaria fragments; Byzantium is a rump around Constantinople; Ottoman beys and sultans take Gallipoli, Adrianople, and push north. Orthodox churches keep Slavic and Greek literacy under rising Islamic rule. This is conquest and conversion pressure on Balkan medieval ancestries — a political–religious transformation with gene flow along armies and slave routes, not a Mesolithic reset.
balkans.languageFamily: South Slavic + Greek + Albanian (emerging in record)
balkans.languages: Serbian/Bulgarian/etc.; Greek; Albanian; Romance islands; Latin in Catholic zones
balkans.linguisticNote: Medieval Balkan multilingualism before Ottoman overlay.
balkans.ancestryNote: Microregional mosaics; schematic continuity with early medieval Balkans.

eastern.culture: Rus’ principalities under Golden Horde pressure
eastern.description: The Golden Horde’s grip loosens; Moscow’s princes collect lands ‘of Rus’’ while Lithuania rules vast Ruthenian Orthodox populations under a pagan-then-Catholic elite. Jogaila’s union with Poland (1386) creates a dual realm facing Teutonic and Muscovite rivals. Steppe politics still matter; deep genetics remain eastern European continua with Turkic–Mongol elite layers.
eastern.languages: Old East Slavic varieties; Turkic; Mongol administration languages
eastern.linguisticNote: Court multilingualism over East Slavic countryside.
eastern.ancestryNote: Medieval East Slavic base + variable steppe/Mongol-era input.

periods.linguistics: Middle English rising in state use; Middle French; Early New High German; Italian vernaculars vs Latin; Castilian/Catalan/Portuguese; Church Slavonic & Ruthenian; Ottoman Turkish administration over Greek/Slavic/Albanian speakers.

GBR.name: Kingdom of England (Hundred Years’ War)
GBR.summary: English kings claim the French crown; longbow armies win Crécy and Agincourt; domestic politics slide toward the Wars of the Roses.
GBR.conflicts: Hundred Years’ War vs France; Scottish wars; Owain Glyndŵr’s Welsh revolt; later York–Lancaster civil war.
GBR.leaders: Edward III; the Black Prince; Richard II; Henry IV; Henry V; Henry VI.
GBR.religion: Latin Christianity under strain of papal Schism; Lollard dissent around Wycliffe’s Bible.
GBR.culture: Chaucer’s English; chivalric orders (Garter); perpendicular Gothic; growing parliamentary bargaining.
GBR.story: Agincourt (1415) becomes England’s mud-and-longbow miracle story — a outnumbered army’s victory that Tudor memory later wraps in nation-myth, even as the French war is eventually lost.
GBR.literature: Chaucer’s pilgrimage comedy, Langland’s vision-politics, Gawain’s green-girdle ethics, Lollard English scripture anxiety. Middle English becomes capable of a nation talking to itself.
GBR.art: Perpendicular Gothic, alabaster saints, illuminated London, plate armour and longbow as English export brands. Dress: livery jackets turning politics into color blocks.

NOR.conflicts: Hansa dominance; black-death demographic shock earlier; loss of Atlantic vigor.
NOR.religion: Catholic archbishopric of Nidaros still prestigious.
NOR.culture: Saga manuscript culture persists; stockfish trade.
NOR.story: Norway’s late medieval arc is quiet tragedy: from independent sea kingdom to junior union partner — reversed only centuries later.
NOR.literature: Dante, Chaucer, Froissart’s chronicles, husite songs, Balkan epic cycles forming around Kosovo, humanist Latin returning in Italian cities. Vernaculars now carry philosophy, insult, and nation-feeling. Norwegian arts remember ships first — keel as national metaphor from Oseberg to oil platforms.
NOR.art: International Gothic, early Netherlandish oil, plate armour couture, Flamboyant stone lace. Dress becomes armor’s soft twin — dagged sleeves and gold chains for a plague-scarred aristocracy. Norwegian arts remember ships first — keel as national metaphor from Oseberg to oil platforms.

periods.label: Reformation & Renaissance
periods.narrative: By the mid-16th century Europe is split by confession and stitched by dynastic empire. Luther, Calvin, and the Catholic Council of Trent redraw belief; print multiplies argument; Habsburgs claim Spain’s global monarchy and the imperial title; Valois then early Bourbon France fights Habsburg encirclement and its own Wars of Religion; Tudor England breaks with Rome; the Ottomans under Süleyman dominate the Balkans and menace Vienna; Ivan IV’s Muscovy becomes an autocratic Orthodox empire; the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth is a noble republic of many faiths; Dutch revolt against Philip II is beginning. Overseas Iberian empires pull silver and souls into European politics. Genetics still sit on medieval continua — conversion and empire move people, but WHG–EEF–steppe deep structure remains.
periods.culturesNote: Habsburg Spain & Austria; Valois France; Tudor England; Lutheran North; Ottoman Rumelia; Muscovy; PLC; Italian Mannerism; Portuguese & Spanish oceans.

iberia.description: Spain under Charles V and Philip II is a composite global monarchy: Castile’s silver fleets, Aragon’s Mediterranean inheritance, Portuguese dynastic entanglement (Iberian Union from 1580). Catholic reform, Inquisition, and expulsion/forced conversion of Muslims and Jews reshape society after Granada’s fall (1492). Culture: Golden Age letters and severe Habsburg piety. Ancestry: medieval Iberia plus Atlantic/imperial contacts — not a new ternary corner.
iberia.linguisticNote: Castilian and Portuguese become world languages from these metropoles.
iberia.ancestryNote: Early modern Iberia ≈ late medieval clines + port diversity; empires transform the Americas more than Iberian deep ancestry.

britain.description: Tudor England — Henry VIII’s break with Rome, Edwardine Protestantism, Mary’s Catholic restoration, Elizabeth’s settlement — invents a national church and fights Spain’s Armada decade. Scotland’s Reformation (Knox) and Ireland’s Tudor conquest wars create three different confessional trajectories on closely related islands. Print, Bible English, and Renaissance humanism redefine elite culture on a late medieval English gene pool.
britain.languages: Early Modern English; Welsh, Irish, Scottish Gaelic, Scots…
britain.ancestryNote: Early modern continuity with medieval Britain; later empire-era migration still limited vs 20th c.

france.description: Valois France oscillates between Italian Wars glory and catastrophic Wars of Religion (Catholic League vs Huguenots) after the 1560s. Royal sacral power meets Calvinist nobles and Parisian radicalism; St Bartholomew’s Day becomes a European trauma story. Art and chateaux of the Renaissance coexist with confessional massacre. Demography is French medieval continuity under extreme political violence.
france.languages: Classical French standardizing; Occitan, Breton, Basque, German dialects, etc.
france.linguisticNote: State language policy begins long pressure on regional langues.
france.ancestryNote: Regional deep structure under one polity label.

central.description: The Holy Roman Empire after the Peace of Augsburg (1555) legalizes cuius regio, eius religio for Lutheran and Catholic princes — a truce before the Thirty Years’ War. Habsburgs hold Austria, Bohemia, Hungary’s remnant against Ottomans; German towns print pamphlets; Swiss cantons host Zwingli/Calvin’s orbits. Culture: confessional schooling, vernacular Bible, and Mannerist courts. Ancestry: central European continua.
central.languages: Early New High German; Czech; Hungarian; Polish; Yiddish; Italian; etc.
central.ancestryNote: Early modern Mitteleuropa continuity + war displacements.

scandinavia.description: Denmark–Norway and Sweden become Lutheran monarchies; Gustav Vasa’s Sweden breaks Kalmar dependency and builds a fiscal-military state. Church lands fund kings; vernacular Bibles standardize speech. Baltic rivalry with Poland and Muscovy replaces union politics. Genetics: Nordic continuity through Reformation institutional change.
scandinavia.linguisticNote: Bible translations and chanceries fix standards.
scandinavia.ancestryNote: Continuous with medieval Norden; great-power wars move armies more than they reset homeland ancestry.

italy.description: Italian wars make the peninsula a Habsburg–Valois battlefield; Spanish Naples and Milan, papal Rome’s Counter-Reformation, Venetian maritime republic, and Tuscan ducal courts define politics. High Renaissance and Mannerism radiate artistic norms across Europe even as political independence wanes. Ancestry: Italian urban–rural medieval mixes with Spanish/Imperial elite overlays.
italy.linguisticNote: Literary Italian without political unity yet.
italy.ancestryNote: Stable north–south structure; ports remain diverse.

balkans.description: Ottoman rule is entrenched across much of the Balkans: timar cavalry, millet confessional autonomy for Orthodox Christians and Jews, Islamization uneven by region (stronger in parts of Bosnia, Albania). Hungarian kingdom is split among Habsburg, Ottoman, and Transylvanian pieces after Mohács (1526). Culture: Orthodox monasteries, Sufi orders, and frontier epics. Genetics: Balkan continua plus Ottoman-era mobility.
balkans.ancestryNote: Elevated “other” as uncertainty band for Ottoman-era inputs; microregional.
balkans.languages: Ottoman Turkish; South Slavic; Greek; Albanian; Romance (e.g. Vlach); others
balkans.linguisticNote: Imperial Turkish + local vernaculars; religion often structures language domains.

eastern.description: Ivan IV (‘the Terrible’) crowns a tsardom, conquers Kazan and Astrakhan, and opens a violent chapter of autocracy and expansion. The Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth (Union of Lublin 1569) is a vast elective noble republic tolerating multiple faiths at elite level while binding Ruthenian lands. Cossack frontiers and Tatar raids frame the steppe edge. Deep ancestry remains eastern European; the novelty is tsarist and Commonwealth institutions.
eastern.languages: Polish; Ruthenian/Ukrainian; Russian; Lithuanian; Yiddish; German; Tatar…
eastern.linguisticNote: PLC nested multilingualism vs Russian imperial centralization later.
eastern.ancestryNote: Slavic-majority demography with Baltic, Finnic, Turkic, and other minorities.

periods.linguistics: Early Modern English; Middle/early modern French; Early New High German; Castilian imperial standard; Italian literary language; Polish & Ruthenian; Church Slavonic/Russian chancery; Ottoman Turkish; Latin still scholarly.

GBR.name: Tudor England (& Reformation Scotland)
GBR.summary: Henry VIII’s royal supremacy, Edward’s Protestant turn, Mary’s Catholic restoration, and Elizabeth’s settlement create a confessional rollercoaster; Scotland adopts a Calvinist kirk.
GBR.conflicts: Rough Wooing vs Scotland; Irish Tudor conquest wars; rivalry with Spain culminating in the Armada (1588).
GBR.leaders: Henry VIII; Edward VI; Mary I; Elizabeth I; Mary Queen of Scots; John Knox.
GBR.religion: Church of England via statute; Catholic underground; Puritan pressure; Scottish Presbyterianism.
GBR.culture: Vernacular Bible and Book of Common Prayer; emerging public theatre (Elizabethan); humanist schools.
GBR.story: The Armada — storm, fireships, and propaganda — becomes Protestant England’s deliverance myth; Mary Queen of Scots’ scaffold is the tragic counter-story of Catholic royalty.
GBR.literature: Tyndale’s English dangers, Cranmer’s Prayer Book music-prose, mid-Tudor polemics, sonnet culture warming toward Elizabethan theatre. Scripture in the mother tongue remakes inward life.
GBR.art: Whitewashed churches, Holbein’s embassy of faces, parade armour for a navy-minded crown. Dress: farthingales and ruffs — Protestant courts still addicted to silk geometry.

periods.label: Early Modern
periods.narrative: Print, Reformation, and composite monarchies: Spanish/Portuguese global empires, France, England→Britain, Habsburgs, Ottoman Europe, Poland–Lithuania, Sweden’s great-power age, rising Russia. Sovereignty and confession redraw maps; deep autosomal structure still echoes Neolithic and Bronze Age pulses, with Ottoman, imperial, and port-city admixture in specific corridors.
periods.culturesNote: Spanish & Portuguese empires, France, England/Britain, Habsburg Mitteleuropa, Ottoman Rumelia, PLC, Sweden, Muscovy/Russia.

iberia.description: Spanish Habsburgs preside over a global monarchy already feeling overstretch: Dutch war, Catalan and Portuguese revolts, literary Golden Age, and American silver. Portugal restores independence in 1640 after Iberian Union. Demography: plague, emigration to empire, and Morisco expulsions earlier reshape society on medieval Iberian ancestries.
iberia.linguisticNote: Castilian and Portuguese become world languages from these metropoles.
iberia.ancestryNote: Early modern Iberia ≈ late medieval clines + port diversity; empires transform the Americas more than Iberian deep ancestry.

britain.description: Union of Crowns (1603) joins Scotland and England under one monarch while Ireland’s conquest and plantation deepen. Civil war, regicide, republic, and Restoration rewrite the meaning of kingship; Navigation Acts and colonies pull the islands into Atlantic empire. Confessional conflict (Anglican, Puritan, Presbyterian, Catholic) is the political language of the century. Genetics: early modern British continua with Irish war demography and growing colonial entanglement — still the medieval ternary at depth.
britain.languages: Early Modern English; Welsh, Irish, Scottish Gaelic, Scots…
britain.ancestryNote: Early modern continuity with medieval Britain; later empire-era migration still limited vs 20th c.

france.description: From Henry IV’s reconstruction through Richelieu and toward Louis XIV, France invents fiscal-military absolutism, tames Huguenot military power, and enters the Thirty Years’ War as a great power. Classical French culture and Versailles politics (later in the century) radiate norms. Ancestry: French medieval continuity under state centralization and war mortality.
france.languages: Classical French standardizing; Occitan, Breton, Basque, German dialects, etc.
france.linguisticNote: State language policy begins long pressure on regional langues.
france.ancestryNote: Regional deep structure under one polity label.

central.description: The Thirty Years’ War guts the Holy Roman Empire; Westphalia (1648) legalizes confessional plurality and strengthens princes. Habsburgs refocus on Austria/Bohemia/Hungary and the Ottoman frontier; Brandenburg rises. Culture: baroque rebuilding on demographic ruin. Genetics: war losses and mobility without a new deep ancestral strand.
central.languages: Early New High German; Czech; Hungarian; Polish; Yiddish; Italian; etc.
central.ancestryNote: Early modern Mitteleuropa continuity + war displacements.

scandinavia.description: Sweden’s great-power century (Gustavus Adolphus to Charles XII’s eve) dominates the Baltic; Denmark–Norway defends the Sound; Finland is Sweden’s eastern wing. Lutheran orthodoxy and military conscription define society. Ancestry: Nordic continua under imperial Swedish extraction of men and copper.
scandinavia.linguisticNote: Bible translations and chanceries fix standards.
scandinavia.ancestryNote: Continuous with medieval Norden; great-power wars move armies more than they reset homeland ancestry.

italy.description: Spanish Habsburg hegemony over Milan and Naples; papal baroque Rome; Venetian twilight; Savoy’s slow rise. Galileo’s trial and baroque art make Italy Europe’s cultural exporter and political dependent. Ancestry: Italian early modern continua with Spanish elite overlays.
italy.linguisticNote: Literary Italian without political unity yet.
italy.ancestryNote: Stable north–south structure; ports remain diverse.

balkans.description: Ottoman rule remains the political frame for much of the Balkans; Habsburg–Ottoman wars pulse along the Military Frontier; Orthodox millets organize Christian life. Islamization varies by region. Genetics: Balkan continua plus frontier resettlements.
balkans.ancestryNote: Elevated “other” as uncertainty band for Ottoman-era inputs; microregional.
balkans.languages: Ottoman Turkish; South Slavic; Greek; Albanian; Romance (e.g. Vlach); others
balkans.linguisticNote: Imperial Turkish + local vernaculars; religion often structures language domains.

eastern.description: Russia exits the Time of Troubles into Romanov consolidation and begins to press Poland and Siberia; the Commonwealth enters the Deluge’s disasters; Cossack uprisings remake Ukraine’s politics. Deep ancestry unchanged in kind; the story is serfdom, autocracy, and noble republic in collision.
eastern.languages: Polish; Ruthenian/Ukrainian; Russian; Lithuanian; Yiddish; German; Tatar…
eastern.linguisticNote: PLC nested multilingualism vs Russian imperial centralization later.
eastern.ancestryNote: Slavic-majority demography with Baltic, Finnic, Turkic, and other minorities.

periods.linguistics: Standardizing national languages; Latin retreats from administration; Ottoman Turkish as imperial language in the Balkans; colonial Spanish/Portuguese/English/French radiate overseas.

ESP.name: Spanish Habsburg monarchy
ESP.conflicts: Dutch Revolt; wars with France/England; Ottoman Mediterranean war.
ESP.leaders: Philip III; Philip IV; Olivares; continuing Habsburg line.
ESP.story: Don Quixote (1605) laughs a tired empire into world literature while silver fleets and bankruptcies continue offstage.
ESP.literature: Cervantes invents the modern novel’s self-awareness; Lope’s theatre ocean; Quevedo’s barbs. An empire declining in cash still rich in sentences.
ESP.art: Velázquez’s mirror games, Zurbarán’s stark saints, still life as theology of objects. Dress and armor in portraits keep claiming a world already slipping.

periods.label: Modern
periods.narrative: Nation-states, industrial demography, world wars, EU integration, and global migration. Present-day Europeans still largely occupy the WHG–EEF–steppe ternary forged before 1000 BCE, with medieval overlays and recent cosmopolitan urban ancestry. Political identity and standard languages change faster than deep genetic clusters — yet fine-scale ancestry remains geographically structured.
periods.culturesNote: European nation-states, post-imperial/post-Soviet east, EU — political map over deep genetic and older linguistic families.

iberia.description: Modern nation-states on Iberian deep history. Autosomal structure still shows north–south and west–east historical clines (including Basque distinctiveness). 20th–21st century immigration diversifies cities without erasing those clines.
iberia.ancestryNote: Present-day averages schematic; urban samples more globally diverse than hinterlands.
iberia.languages: Spanish, Portuguese, Catalan, Galician, Basque, etc.

britain.description: UK and Ireland. Fine-scale genetic structure (e.g. People of the British Isles) often echoes early medieval kingdoms more than Victorian counties. English globally dominant; Celtic languages in minority/revitalization contexts; recent global immigration overlays cities.
britain.languages: English; Welsh, Irish, Scottish Gaelic, Scots…
britain.linguisticNote: English as global language from this islands’ modern history.
britain.ancestryNote: Early medieval structure still readable; urban cosmopolitanism recent.

france.description: Centralized republic with persistent regional deep structure and languages under pressure from French. 20th–21st c. immigration diversifies metros. Genetics still track older north/south and peripheral patterns beneath national identity.
france.languages: French; Breton, Basque, Occitan, Alsatian…; immigrant languages
france.linguisticNote: Strong standard-language ideology; regional revitalization movements.
france.ancestryNote: Regional structure + modern migration in cities.

central.description: Modern Central European states after empires and 20th-century border violence. Ancestry continuous with early modern Mitteleuropa plus displacements and recent migration. National labels sit on older German–Slavic–Uralic (Hungarian) mosaics.
central.languages: German, Polish, Czech, Slovak, Hungarian, etc.
central.linguisticNote: Nation-state languages after Habsburg/German/Russian imperial frames.
central.ancestryNote: Post-imperial continuity + 20th c. forced migrations + recent immigration.

scandinavia.description: Denmark, Norway, Sweden, Iceland (and Finland as Uralic neighbor in the wider north). Deep continuity from Iron/Viking Age in Germanic Scandinavia; recent international migration in cities. Finland’s Finnish language is Uralic, not IE — important map-edge exception.
scandinavia.linguisticNote: IE North Germanic bloc beside Uralic Finnish.

italy.description: Political unification overlays a deep north–south genetic and dialect continuum that still structures variation more than the modern state alone. Italian standard from Tuscan; dialects remain strong. Recent immigration adds urban diversity.
italy.linguisticNote: Standard Italian over a dialect continuum.
italy.ancestryNote: Strong north–south cline (ancient/medieval); modern migration in cities.

balkans.description: Post-Ottoman and post-Yugoslav nations. Genetic structure is finely regional; religion and standard languages imperfectly match ancestry. South Slavic, Greek, Albanian, Romance (Romanian), and Turkish-speaking communities intertwine.
balkans.languageFamily: South Slavic + Greek + Albanian + Romance + Turkish
balkans.languages: Greek, Bulgarian, BCMS, Albanian, Romanian, Turkish, etc.
balkans.linguisticNote: A shatterbelt of national standards after Ottoman and Yugoslav frames; language and religion borders only loosely track ancestry.
balkans.ancestryNote: Local mosaics; nation averages hide village-scale history.

eastern.description: Poland, Baltics, Belarus, Ukraine, western Russia, and neighbors. Broad east–west genetic clines; steppe and forest histories still readable. 20th-century wars, deportations, and border changes move people; deep ternary ancestry remains the backdrop to modern politics.
eastern.languageFamily: East Slavic + Baltic + West Slavic + others
eastern.languages: Russian, Ukrainian, Belarusian, Polish, Baltic languages, etc.
eastern.linguisticNote: Imperial and Soviet language politics still shape the map.
eastern.ancestryNote: East Slavic/Baltic/West Slavic structure + historical minorities; modern upheavals.

periods.linguistics: State standards (and co-official minorities), immigrant languages in cities, English as European lingua franca. Families remain Indo-European almost everywhere, with Basque and Uralic (Finnish/Hungarian/Estonian) as major non-IE exceptions in this map’s frame.

FIN.name: Republic of Finland
FIN.summary: Independent since 1917; Nordic democracy beside Russia.
FIN.conflicts: Winter War and Continuation War memory; EU/NATO era security politics.
FIN.leaders: Mannerheim in founding memory; post-war presidents; contemporary cabinets.
FIN.culture: Sisu myth; design; bilingual Finnish/Swedish legacy.
FIN.story: The Winter War — tiny Finland holding the Red Army — remains the national epic of survival.
FIN.literature: National canons, modernist fracture, postcolonial argument, EU multilingual culture industries. Poetry and novels become the museum of feelings nations tell about themselves — and argue with. Finnish oral epic (later Kalevala) and modern design both treat forest silence as a material.
FIN.art: From industrial sublime to Impressionism to contemporary biennales; folk costume revived as heritage; military uniform as the last total clothing system. Dress democratizes while brands feudalize desire. Finnish oral epic (later Kalevala) and modern design both treat forest silence as a material.

POL.culture: Romantic independence tradition; EU mobility; war memory (WW2).
POL.story: Shipyard strikes in Gdańsk (1980) begin the crack in the Eastern Bloc — a trade union that helped end an empire.
POL.literature: Romantic messianism, Miłosz and Szymborska’s moral clarity, reportage traditions — literature as national nervous system under partitions and party.
POL.art: Poster art genius, Chopin’s export ghost, Solidarity’s graphic simple courage. Hussar wings return as heritage cosplay and meme.

RUS.name: Russian Federation
RUS.conflicts: Chechen wars; Georgia 2008; Ukraine wars — ongoing regional conflict.
RUS.leaders: Soviet general secretaries in memory; Yeltsin; Putin-era presidency.
RUS.religion: Orthodox revival after Soviet atheism; minorities of many faiths.
RUS.culture: High literary canon; petro-state geopolitics; Soviet memory wars.
RUS.story: 1991’s flag over the Kremlin ends the USSR; the post-Soviet story is unresolved empire, oligarchy, and war — still rewriting Europe’s map.
RUS.literature: Pushkin to Tolstoy to Soviet and post-Soviet argument — a literature that treats the soul as a public utility and a crime scene.
RUS.art: Icons to Malevich to film montage; monumentalism and its mockers. Dress: imperial parade vs Soviet uniformity vs oligarch gloss.

UKR.name: Ukraine
UKR.leaders: Post-1991 presidents; Maidan-era civic leadership; wartime presidency.
UKR.religion: Orthodox jurisdictions in flux; Greek Catholic west; pluralism.
UKR.culture: Language politics; Cossack memory; European aspiration.
UKR.story: Maidan (2014) and full-scale invasion (2022) make Ukraine’s sovereignty the defining European story of the early 21st century.
UKR.literature: National canons, modernist fracture, postcolonial argument, EU multilingual culture industries. Poetry and novels become the museum of feelings nations tell about themselves — and argue with. Borderland creativity — Cossack, Ruthenian, and European currents braided under dangerous skies.
UKR.art: From industrial sublime to Impressionism to contemporary biennales; folk costume revived as heritage; military uniform as the last total clothing system. Dress democratizes while brands feudalize desire. Borderland creativity — Cossack, Ruthenian, and European currents braided under dangerous skies.
